register.description: This register provides the highest priority enabled interrupt index. 0x00. means no event pending, 0x01 means interrupt pending for channel 0, 0x07 means interrupt pending for channel 6. Interrupt 1 is the highest priority, 2 next highest, 3,4, ...,7 is the least priority. That is, the least bit position that is set to 1 denotes the highest priority pending interrupt. channel 1 has highest priority, channel 6 has lowest. On each read, only one interrupt is indicated. On a read, the current interrupt (highest priority) is automatically cleared by the hardware and the corresponding interrupt flag in the RIS and MIS are cleared as well. After a read from the CPU (not from the debug interface), the register must be updated with the next highest priority interrupt, if none are pending, then it should display 0h

destination padding pattern. This field has only an effect if block_mode_dest is asserted. If the number of bytes provided is not sufficient to complete 1 block, the DMA engine shall pad the remaining bytes to provide 1 full block of data to the accelerator. Some of the accelerators already support a subset of padding schemes, hence a partial last block is not necessarily an error. Note that FIPS andf RFC are in big endian. See crypto engine documentation for details.
0: No Padding. If the DMA is unable to transfer a full word (and also finish a block), it must keep up to 3 bytes that were already read in a buffer. Once the next pointer (gather function) is programed (automatically or by the software), it resumes filling up words to complete a block. The buffer is cleared (might be a simple pointer re-init) by setting the init field to 1. 1: (Poly1305, AES-CCM) all zeros. 2: (AES-CMAC) 0x80 followed by all zeros. 3: (SHAKE) pad10*1. Depending on the rate (r=1600-c), the DMA forms an integer multiple of r. Message || 0x1F || 00...0 || 0x80. The DMA adds a 0x1F (for SHAKE) after the last byte of the message, then all 0s, then 0x80 at the last byte. 4: Pad with 0x01, 0x02, 0x03,...,0xn (where n is the number of padding bytes) (TBD as this one might very complex to implement along with the byte realignment requirement) 5: All zeros except for the last byte which says how many bytes of padding there are (ANSI X.923). E.g. 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x04 6: Pad with repeated byte stating how many padding bytes there are (PKCS#7 https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5652#section-6.3). E.g. 0x03 0x03 0x03 7: Pad with padding length. TLS padding: https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc5246.txt. Message + mac + padding length + padding length repeated. E.g. xx 0x03 0x03 0x03 0x03. (see section 6.2.3.2. of the link above for a full explanation).

destination padding pattern. This field has only an effect if block_mode_dest is asserted. If the number of bytes provided is not sufficient to complete 1 block, the DMA engine shall pad the remaining bytes to provide 1 full block of data to the accelerator. Some of the accelerators already support a subset of padding schemes, hence a partial last block is not necessarily an error. Note that FIPS andf RFC are in big endian. See crypto engine documentation for details.
0: No Padding. If the DMA is unable to transfer a full word (and also finish a block), it must keep up to 3 bytes that were already read in a buffer. Once the next pointer (gather function) is programed (automatically or by the software), it resumes filling up words to complete a block. The buffer is cleared (might be a simple pointer re-init) by setting the init field to 1. 1: (Poly1305, AES-CCM) all zeros. 2: (AES-CMAC) 0x80 followed by all zeros. 3: (SHAKE) pad10*1. Depending on the rate (r=1600-c), the DMA forms an integer multiple of r. Message || 0x1F || 00...0 || 0x80. The DMA adds a 0x1F (for SHAKE) after the last byte of the message, then all 0s, then 0x80 at the last byte. 4: Pad with 0x01, 0x02, 0x03,...,0xn (where n is the number of padding bytes) (TBD as this one might very complex to implement along with the byte realignment requirement) 5: All zeros except for the last byte which says how many bytes of padding there are (ANSI X.923). TLS padding: https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc5246.txt. Message + mac + padding length + padding length repeated. E.g. xx 0x03 0x03 0x03 0x03. (see section 6.2.3.2. of the link above for a full explanation).

(The length of the message goes in 449-512). SHA-384, 512 http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf (5.1.2) -Append 1 bit, zero out to the 896th/1024th bit.

destination padding pattern. This field has only an effect if block_mode_dest is asserted. If the number of bytes provided is not sufficient to complete 1 block, the DMA engine shall pad the remaining bytes to provide 1 full block of data to the accelerator. Some of the accelerators already support a subset of padding schemes, hence a partial last block is not necessarily an error. Note that FIPS andf RFC are in big endian. See crypto engine documentation for details.
0: No Padding. If the DMA is unable to transfer a full word (and also finish a block), it must keep up to 3 bytes that were already read in a buffer. Once the next pointer (gather function) is programed (automatically or by the software), it resumes filling up words to complete a block. The buffer is cleared (might be a simple pointer re-init) by setting the init field to 1. 1: (Poly1305, AES-CCM) all zeros. 2: (AES-CMAC) 0x80 followed by all zeros. 3: (SHAKE) pad10*1. Depending on the rate (r=1600-c), the DMA forms an integer multiple of r. Message || 0x1F || 00...0 || 0x80. The DMA adds a 0x1F (for SHAKE) after the last byte of the message, then all 0s, then 0x80 at the last byte. 4: Pad with 0x01, 0x02, 0x03,...,0xn (where n is the number of padding bytes) (TBD as this one might very complex to implement along with the byte realignment requirement) 5: All zeros except for the last byte which says how many bytes of padding there are (ANSI X.923). (see section 6.2.3.2. of the link above for a full explanation).
